idiom_name: hand-written forwarding method; #[inline] for cross-crate inlining
implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance and no delegation clause, so a named operation is written explicitly - pub fn cancel_order(&self, id: OrderId) -> Result<CancelResult> { self.repo.cancel(id) } - either in an inherent impl or inside a trait impl when the method must satisfy a bound. #[inline] exists mainly so a non-generic body is available to other crates (generic functions are instantiated where they are used and do not need it); it is a hint the optimizer may ignore. Deref looks like automatic delegation - a wrapper implicitly gets the target's &self methods - but the standard library documents it as appropriate only when the wrapper transparently behaves like the target and warns against collision-prone method sets, so it is not the delegation feature it appears to be; wrapper-forwarding macros are the remaining option when a whole trait must be forwarded.
pitfalls: Deref makes method lookup silently fall through to the target and is part of the public API: the std docs list methods likely to collide with the target's as a reason not to implement it.
#[inline(always)] is a hint the optimizer may ignore and can bloat code; plain #[inline] matters mainly across crate boundaries, so do not scatter it on every one-liner.

The orphan rule forbids implementing a foreign trait for a foreign type, so a wrapper newtype plus hand-written one-liners (or a macro) is the only way to satisfy a bound the delegate cannot satisfy directly.
